heroTitle: Installable expert flows for every AI coding tool you use.
heroBody: FlaiOS Agents is the agent shelf for your AI Flow OS: code review, product design, growth, data, operations, and safety specialists packaged for Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, VSCode, Trae, and portable AGENTS.md workflows.
heroSubline: Stop rewriting prompts and moving habits by hand. Pick one agent or a flow pack, then let every AI call run through a clearer, controlled workflow.
packsTitle: Install a coordinated AI workflow, not a lonely prompt.

usage.title: FlaiOS Agents is not another chat box. It is the control layer for the tools you already use.
usage.body: The website helps you browse, filter, and copy install commands. The actual work happens in Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, VSCode Copilot, Trae, and similar tools. Each agent is a readable, auditable, portable workflow file.

steps.title: Choose
steps.body: Pick a focused specialist, or install a flow pack such as solo-founder-pack or code-quality-pack.

steps.title: Install
steps.body: Copy the generated command and write the agent files into your project or target tool config directory.

steps.title: Run
steps.body: Return to the target AI tool and describe the task naturally; the generated agent, rule, or skill constrains the workflow, outputs, and safety boundary.

usage.noteBody: These agents are Lao Zhou's everyday workflows, updated whenever real work exposes a better pattern. Take what helps, install it directly, and adapt it to your own tools and projects.

codex.where: Install as Codex skills, then call the specialist by task intent inside Codex.
notes: Best for repo work, code review, debugging, research workflows, and repeatable local tasks.
Use collections when you want a ready-made working team instead of one specialist.

claude.where: Install as Claude Code subagent markdown files under .claude/agents.
notes: Best for subagent-style delegation inside a project.
Generated files are portable markdown, so you can inspect and edit them.

cursor.where: Install as Cursor rule files under .cursor/rules.
notes: Best for project-level behavior presets and repeatable coding rules.
Use focused agents for review, frontend, backend, product, and naming tasks.

opencode.where: Install as OpenCode agent markdown under .opencode/agents.
notes: Best for terminal-native workflows and repository assistants.
Use --target all if you want to prepare every platform at once.
Best for project instructions that travel with the repo.
Keep sensitive or personal workflow rules out of public repos.

trae.where: Install as Trae-compatible prompt markdown under .trae/agents.
notes: Best for product, growth, Chinese-market, and coding assistant workflows.
The generated prompt remains readable and editable.

scenePanel.title: Find agents by real work scenes, then refine with tags.
scenePanel.body: Categories organize the repository, but users search by jobs like Douyin ops, A-share T0, short-drama production, overseas social, or game development. Scenario view makes those entry points primary while tags keep discovery precise.
scenePanel.allBody: Browse the full agent shelf, then narrow by category, search, and target platform.

aiTools.title: Choose AI-native tools by work scene, not just by brand name.
aiTools.body: This channel organizes AI-native editors, AI IDEs, chat tools, and automation tools by fit, operating method, and selection boundary.
aiTools.noteBody: This page is a scene-based tool map, not a replacement for the agent shelf. Later it can grow into reviews, install guides, and workflow templates.

groups.title: AI-native editors
groups.body: Best when AI belongs inside docs, knowledge bases, decks, and content workflows.
bestFor: Meeting notes, plans, and knowledge bases
Marketing content, decks, and public materials
howToUse: Put audience, structure, and source material in one document
Generate a draft, then verify facts and add judgment
Save stable patterns as templates or team standards

groups.title: AI IDEs and coding assistants
groups.body: Best for feature work, review, refactors, tests, and debugging inside real repositories.
bestFor: Complex bug investigation and test coverage
howToUse: Start with README, tests, and key modules
Break work into verifiable steps and run build or test
Install Lazy Agent Shelf agents to make the workflow repeatable

groups.title: AI chat tools
groups.body: Best for open-ended discussion, source understanding, model comparison, and direction setting.
howToUse: State context, goal, constraints, and output format up front
Ask for sources or verification paths for factual claims
Move complex execution into an IDE or agent workflow

groups.title: AI automation and browser agents
groups.body: Best for repeatable work that crosses pages, forms, apps, and APIs.
howToUse: Run the manual flow once and record every checkpoint
Keep accounts, permissions, and sensitive actions human-approved
Start read-only, then add writes and submissions gradually

models.title: Keep only ten top models so the choice stays usable.
models.body: This editorial list favors broad capability, ecosystem availability, and real workflow coverage instead of long-tail model dumping.
models.noteBody: Ranking is editorial: check public leaderboards, official releases, and hands-on availability before publishing a strict leaderboard version.

items.name: OpenAI GPT-5.5
items.body: Flagship general model for complex reasoning, coding, tool use, and multimodal workflows.

items.name: Anthropic Claude Opus 4.5
items.body: Strong for long context, writing, code review, and agentic repository work.

items.name: Google Gemini 3 Pro
items.body: Strong multimodal and large-context option, especially around Google ecosystem work.

items.name: xAI Grok 4
items.body: Useful for real-time context, social signals, and fast exploratory reasoning.

items.name: DeepSeek R2
items.body: Worth tracking for Chinese, coding, and cost-sensitive workflows.

items.name: Qwen 3 Max
items.body: Strong Chinese ecosystem model for business, content, and tool-calling applications.

items.name: Meta Llama 4
items.body: Core open ecosystem option for private deployment, tuning, and controllable stacks.

items.name: Mistral Large 3
items.body: Enterprise-friendly European model family for multilingual and low-latency use cases.

items.name: Cohere Command R+

items.name: Perplexity Sonar
items.body: Research-oriented model entry point for web-grounded answers with source trails.

aiStarter.title: When a friend asks how to use AI, start with their type.
aiStarter.body: No long lecture. Pick the person type, then show a demo that produces value in 10 minutes.

personas.label: Some technical base / reads code
personas.title: Use an AI IDE to unlock the most capability
personas.body: Do not keep them in chat. Codex, VSCode Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code can read files, edit code, run tests, and connect work across the computer.
personas.demo: Open a small repo, ask Codex to read the README, add one button, and run the build.
steps: Prepare a real folder or Git repo
Ask AI to explain the structure first
Give one small change and require build/test verification

personas.label: No technical base / only chats
personas.title: Move from chat loops to deliverable loops
personas.body: They know ask-and-reply, but need context, goal, materials, and output format so AI returns copy, tables, checklists, or emails.
personas.demo: Paste a product idea into ChatGPT/Claude and ask for title, selling points, social post, and customer Q&A.
steps: Iterate with shorter, more casual, or table format

personas.label: Business / ops / managers
personas.title: Find the first AI cut inside repeated work
personas.body: They may not code, but they own workflows, spreadsheets, customer messages, and decisions. Start with reports, reviews, spreadsheet analysis, SOPs, or meeting notes.
personas.demo: Give AI a sales record and ask for anomalies, risky customers, and next-week follow-ups.
steps: Pick a task repeated more than twice a week
Provide a real sample and ideal output
Turn the result into a reusable template
